body:
Theatre as a composite performing art

Theatre is a form of storytelling in which performers represent characters, actions and situations before an audience. It combines acting, dialogue, music, dance, costumes, make-up and other artistic elements. For this reason, theatre is described as a composite art form.

Indian theatrical traditions developed through religious ceremonies, festivals, court performances, community gatherings and popular entertainment. The Ramayana, Mahabharata, Puranas, regional legends, historical events and ordinary social life have all provided material for theatrical performances.

Indian theatre can be understood through 3 broad traditions:

  • Classical theatre: Theatre associated with Sanskrit dramatic literature, established principles of performance and classical dramatic traditions.
  • Traditional and folk theatre: Regional performances that use local languages, music, humour, religious narratives and community customs. Bhavai of Gujarat and Nautanki of Uttar Pradesh are examples.
  • Modern theatre: Theatre influenced by modern literary movements, professional stage companies, social reform, nationalism and changing approaches to dramatic presentation.

These traditions are not mutually exclusive historical stages. Classical, folk and modern forms continue to coexist and influence one another.

The Natyashastra

The Natyashastra, traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni, is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian dramaturgy and performing arts. Its compilation took place over a long period, and scholars do not agree on a single exact date for its composition.

It deals with dramatic composition, acting, emotional expression, dance, music, costumes, theatrical architecture and the relationship between performers and audiences. Its influence extends beyond theatre to several Indian classical dance traditions.

Traditional account of the origin of drama

According to the account contained in the Natyashastra, Brahma created Natya by drawing elements from the 4 Vedas:

  • Rigveda: Recitation or spoken text.
  • Samaveda: Music and song.
  • Yajurveda: Acting and expressive action.
  • Atharvaveda: Rasa or aesthetic experience.

Drama is therefore traditionally described as the Natya Veda or the fifth Veda. This is a traditional explanation of the sacred and inclusive character of drama, rather than evidence that a separate fifth Vedic collection was historically composed.

Rasa and Bhava

Bhava refers to an emotional state or feeling expressed through performance. Rasa is the aesthetic experience that arises in the audience when these emotions and dramatic situations are effectively presented.

For example, the representation of a character's suffering may produce an experience of compassion or sorrow in the audience. The emotion represented by the performer and the aesthetic experience received by the audience are related but distinct.

RasaAssociated experience
ShringaraLove and beauty
HasyaHumour and laughter
KarunaSorrow and compassion
RaudraAnger and fury
ViraHeroism and courage
BhayanakaFear
BibhatsaDisgust
AdbhutaWonder
ShantaPeace and tranquillity

The original enumeration conventionally associated with Bharata contains 8 rasas. Shanta became widely accepted as the ninth rasa through later aesthetic thought. The collective expression Navarasa refers to the 9 rasas.

The 4 forms of Abhinaya

Abhinaya is the communication of dramatic meaning through performance. The classical tradition distinguishes 4 principal forms:

  • Angika: Expression through bodily movements, gestures and facial expressions.
  • Vachika: Expression through speech, dialogue, recitation and song.
  • Aharya: Expression through costumes, make-up, ornaments and other visual elements.
  • Sattvika: Expression of inner emotional states through manifestations such as tears, trembling or changes in expression.

Other important classical treatises

TextAuthorSubject
NatyashastraBharata MuniDramaturgy and performing arts
AbhinavabharatiAbhinavaguptaCommentary on the Natyashastra
DasharupakaDhananjaya10 types of dramatic composition
Abhinaya DarpanaNandikeshvaraExpressive movement and gestures, particularly in dance

Abhinavagupta, a scholar associated with Kashmir, made important contributions to the interpretation of rasa, including the discussion of Shanta rasa.

Prelims focus

  • Natyashastra is traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni.
  • Abhinavabharati is Abhinavagupta's commentary on the Natyashastra.
  • Dasharupaka was composed by Dhananjaya.
  • The 4 forms of Abhinaya are Angika, Vachika, Aharya and Sattvika.
  • Shanta is conventionally regarded as the ninth rasa.
  • Trap: Bhava is an expressed emotional state, whereas rasa is the resulting aesthetic experience.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, pp. 112–115; CBSE, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Class 11, Module 10: Theatre and Drama in India, sections on the Natyashastra and Sanskrit theatre; Central Sanskrit University, Sanskrit and the Arts, Theatre section; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Indian Theatre: Origins, Nature and the Natyashastra

body:
Characteristics of Sanskrit drama

Classical Sanskrit theatre represents an important part of ancient Indian literary and performing traditions. Its dramatic literature includes stories of royal life, romance, political conflict, ethical dilemmas and episodes adapted from the great epics.

Although it is called Sanskrit theatre, its plays often contain both Sanskrit and Prakrit. Sanskrit was generally associated with learned and high-status characters, while different forms of Prakrit were used by several other characters. The selection of language depended on dramatic conventions, social identity and the context of the play.

Important dramatic terms

  • Sutradhara: The stage manager or presenter who commonly introduces the dramatic performance.
  • Nandi: An auspicious or benedictory verse associated with the beginning of a play.
  • Vidushaka: A comic character, often a companion of the hero, whose humour provides entertainment and sometimes social commentary.
  • Nataka: A dramatic form commonly based on an established story, such as an epic narrative or the life of a well-known hero.
  • Prakarana: A dramatic form generally based on a plot devised by the playwright, often involving ordinary social life.

Classical Sanskrit drama commonly favoured auspicious resolutions. However, this was not an absolute feature of every surviving play. Bhasa's Urubhanga, which depicts the tragic fate of Duryodhana, is a notable exception.

Bhasa

Bhasa was an early Sanskrit dramatist who preceded Kalidasa. His exact historical period remains uncertain. Many of his plays adapt stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and other established narrative traditions.

Svapnavasavadatta concerns King Udayana and Queen Vasavadatta. Pratijnayaugandharayana also deals with Udayana and his minister Yaugandharayana. Urubhanga and Karnabhara draw upon the Mahabharata.

Kalidasa

Kalidasa is celebrated as both a Sanskrit poet and dramatist and is commonly associated with the Gupta age, although his precise dates are uncertain.

  • Abhijnanashakuntalam: The story of Shakuntala and King Dushyanta, adapted from the Mahabharata.
  • Malavikagnimitram: A romantic drama involving Agnimitra, a ruler of the Shunga dynasty, and Malavika.
  • Vikramorvashiyam: The story of King Pururavas and the celestial maiden Urvashi.

Kalidasa also composed important poetic works, including Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha and Kumarasambhava. These must be distinguished from his plays.

Other important Sanskrit playwrights

PlaywrightImportant worksPrincipal association
ShudrakaMrichchhakatikaUrban society, romance and political conflict
VishakhadattaMudrarakshasaChanakya and Chandragupta Maurya
BhavabhutiMahaviracharita, Uttararamacharita, MalatimadhavaEpic narratives and romance
HarshaRatnavali, Priyadarshika, NaganandaRoyal romance and ethical themes

Mrichchhakatika and Mudrarakshasa

Mrichchhakatika, meaning The Little Clay Cart, is traditionally attributed to Shudraka. It depicts the relationship between Charudatta and Vasantasena against a background of urban social and political life. It is an important example of Prakarana.

Mudrarakshasa, written by Vishakhadatta, is a political drama concerning the establishment and consolidation of Chandragupta Maurya's power with the assistance of Chanakya. Its title refers to Rakshasa, the minister whom Chanakya seeks to win over.

Mudrarakshasa concerns events associated with the beginning of the Mauryan Empire, but that does not establish that the playwright himself lived during Chandragupta Maurya's reign. The historical setting of a drama must be distinguished from its period of composition.

Bhavabhuti and Harsha

Bhavabhuti is generally placed in the 8th century CE. Mahaviracharita presents the earlier life of Rama, while Uttararamacharita concerns the later part of Rama's life. Malatimadhava is a romantic drama.

Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda are traditionally attributed to Harshavardhana, the 7th-century ruler associated with Thanesar and Kannauj. Nagananda contains the story of Jimutavahana and is notable for its Buddhist ethical associations.

Distinguish the authors

Shudraka wrote Mrichchhakatika, while Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa. Kalidasa wrote Malavikagnimitram, while Bhavabhuti wrote Malatimadhava. Similar-looking titles do not indicate common authorship.

Prelims focus

  • Bhasa: Svapnavasavadatta, Urubhanga and Karnabhara.
  • Kalidasa: Abhijnanashakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvashiyam.
  • Shudraka: Mrichchhakatika.
  • Vishakhadatta: Mudrarakshasa.
  • Bhavabhuti: Uttararamacharita and Malatimadhava.
  • Trap: Meghaduta is a poem, not a dramatic composition.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Buildings, Paintings and Books, pp. 127–129; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10 Social Science, English edition, Literary Heritage of India, p. 31; CBSE, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Class 11, Module 10: Theatre and Drama in India, Sanskrit drama section; Central Sanskrit University, Sanskrit and the Arts, Theatre section. External textbook copy used because the project Volume 09 chapter pages were unreadable; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Classical Sanskrit Theatre and Major Playwrights

body:
Nature of traditional folk theatre

Folk theatre is a community-oriented dramatic tradition that reflects the language, beliefs, customs and experiences of a region. It commonly combines dialogue, singing, dancing, humour and narration.

Many folk theatre forms developed around temples, fairs, festivals, village gatherings and travelling performance groups. Performers frequently address the audience directly, adapt familiar narratives and incorporate contemporary social issues.

Unlike formal Sanskrit dramatic literature, folk theatre commonly uses regional languages and dialects. Its repertoire may be transmitted orally, through written scripts or through a combination of both methods.

Northern Indian theatre traditions

Ramlila and Raslila

Ramlila is the dramatic enactment of the story of Rama. In northern India, many Ramlila traditions draw their narrative from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Performances commonly take place around the Dussehra festival.

Important Ramlila centres include Ayodhya and Ramnagar near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh. Some traditions extend over several days and involve extensive community participation.

Raslila is associated particularly with the Braj region, including Mathura and Vrindavan. It combines devotional music, dance and drama to represent episodes from the life of Krishna, especially his childhood and relationship with the Gopis.

Other northern forms

Theatre formPrincipal regionIdentifying feature
Bhand PatherKashmirComedy, satire, music and social commentary
Swang or SaangHaryana and adjoining northern regionsSung narratives and dramatic dialogue
NautankiUttar PradeshPopular musical theatre with romantic, heroic and social stories

Bhand Pather is associated with traditional Bhand performers. Satire and parody allow them to represent the conduct of different sections of society.

Nautanki developed important centres at Hathras and Kanpur. Gulab Bai was a prominent exponent associated with Kanpur Nautanki and contributed to the visibility of women performers in this tradition.

Swang and Nautanki are closely related musical theatre traditions. Their regional associations are useful for identification, but their geographical distribution is not restricted strictly to the borders of one state.

Western and central Indian traditions

Theatre formPrincipal regionIdentifying feature
BhavaiGujaratSatirical sketches, humour and devotional elements
KhyalRajasthanMusical drama based on popular legends and religious stories
MaachMalwa, Madhya PradeshSong-dominated folk theatre
TamashaMaharashtraPopular musical entertainment, dance and comedy
DashavataraKonkan and GoaStories of the 10 incarnations of Vishnu

The word Maach is associated with both the stage and the theatrical form. Songs occupy a prominent place in its dramatic presentation.

Tamasha has a strong association with Marathi popular culture. Lavani, a Marathi tradition of song and dance, is an important element in many Tamasha performances. However, Lavani itself is not identical to the complete theatrical form of Tamasha.

Dashavatara combines religious narratives with dramatic presentation. It is particularly associated with the coastal Konkan region and Goa rather than with a single inland state.

Eastern and northeastern traditions

Jatra

Jatra is a popular theatre tradition of Bengal, also found in adjoining regions, including Odisha. Its development is closely connected with religious processions, festivals and devotional performances.

The influence of Chaitanya contributed to the popularity of Krishna-centred devotional narratives in Bengal. Over time, Jatra expanded to include historical, romantic, social and political themes. Music, powerful dialogue and dramatic presentation remain important features.

Ankiya Naat and Bhaona

Ankiya Naat refers to the devotional one-act dramatic compositions associated with the Assamese Vaishnava saint and reformer Srimanta Sankaradeva.

These plays communicate religious ideas through music, narration and dramatic enactment. Brajavali, a literary language associated with Assamese Vaishnava compositions, is an important linguistic feature of this tradition.

Bhaona refers to the theatrical presentation of Ankiya Naat. The tradition has strong links with Assamese religious institutions, including Namghars, which are community prayer halls, and Satras, which are Vaishnava religious and cultural institutions.

Play and performance

Ankiya Naat identifies the dramatic composition, while Bhaona identifies its performance tradition. Both are associated with Assam and Sankaradeva's Vaishnava movement.

Bidesia

Bidesia is a Bhojpuri theatrical tradition associated with Bihar and the playwright-performer Bhikhari Thakur. It is known particularly for presenting migration, separation of families and social problems through music, drama and humour.

Prelims focus

  • Bhand Pather: Kashmir; Nautanki: Uttar Pradesh; Swang: Haryana and adjoining regions.
  • Bhavai: Gujarat; Maach: Madhya Pradesh; Tamasha: Maharashtra.
  • Jatra is principally associated with Bengal.
  • Ankiya Naat and Bhaona are associated with Sankaradeva and Assam.
  • Bidesia is associated with Bhikhari Thakur and Bhojpuri theatre.
  • Trap: Ramlila presents Rama's story, whereas Raslila principally presents Krishna's life.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, pp. 112–113; CCRT, Traditional Theatre Forms of India, Cultural Package 17; Employment News, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Different Forms of Traditional Theatre, 25–31 March 2023; IGNCA, Intangible Cultural Heritage Inventory, Nautanki; UNESCO, Ramlila, the Traditional Performance of the Ramayana; CBSE, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Class 11, Module 10, regional theatre sections; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
